files.prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept.
Asset type: original, production-quality opaque vertical scrolling background for a high-altitude airplane action game, 1024x1536 portrait. One complete painting, edge to edge, no contact sheet.

Image 1 is a STYLE REFERENCE ONLY: the project's approved painted first-stage island. Match its broad, gentle brush planes, clean readable light and shadow, slightly soft hand-painted anime environmental rendering, and miniature aerial scale. Replace its tropical subject with a polar environment. Do not reuse the island outline or its water composition.

Create a vast frozen icefield with an understated small Inuit-style snow-block igloo camp integrated into the snow. The camera looks almost straight down from high altitude, around 75–80 degrees downward, with no horizon. Top surfaces dominate, only very shallow edges or building sides are visible. This is a scrolling aerial battlefield, not an isometric diorama, postcard, landscape vista, or a close-up of buildings.

COMPOSITION: A wide, quiet slate-blue and desaturated teal frozen ice surface occupies most of the image, especially the central 55 percent. The center is solid old blue ice with broad painterly patches, subtle trapped frost, and a few thin irregular pale cracks. Place snow-covered ice shelves and shallow drifts in asymmetrical, offset clusters towards the sides. A branching deep navy fissure occupies the upper right edge, with only a little open water and a few low broken ice plates nearby. The icefield should feel broad and continuous; avoid a long central river bounded by two symmetrical shores. Avoid a road, lane markings, a straight canyon, or a central decorative island.

CAMP: On a low left-edge snow shelf in the lower-middle portion, place a tiny grounded cluster of three modest snow-block dome igloos. Each igloo has a low round roof made from quiet snow blocks, a short low tunnel entrance, blue contact shade, and a dusting of windblown snow. The entire camp is only about 12–15 percent of the image width; each igloo is roughly 3–5 percent of image width. Include a very small sled and a couple of bundled supplies close to the entrances, faint short footprints, and a small orange tarp or warm doorway as a restrained accent. No people, no caricatures, no costumes, no totem poles. Integrate everything into the same ground painting with coherent contact shadows and partly buried bases. Do not make separate objects look pasted onto the ice.

TERRAIN: Snow is muted ivory and cool silver-blue rather than glaring pure white. Ice has broad translucent dark-cyan color planes, restrained edge reflections, no ocean-wave texture, no dense glitter, no lava-like glowing cracks. Use low rounded snow berms, shallow fractured shelves, sparse dark rocks, no forest, no tall crystalline spires, no towering cliff walls. Details must be small relative to the playable field. Preserve quiet low-contrast space through the middle so aircraft and bright bullets stay legible.

LIGHT: The same soft upper-left daylight and gentle blue-gray shadows as the reference, with subtle aerial softness. Clean and cohesive, lightly textured painted surfaces. No photographic microdetail, no plastic 3D toy shading, no thick outlines, no dirty grunge filter.

SCROLLING: At both the top and bottom edges, keep similar quiet blue ice through the middle and low snow clusters near the lateral edges, with no big object cut across a horizontal seam. Vary the coastline/drift outlines naturally; do not add horizontal roads, bars, borders, or a wide horizontal strip.

Do not bake in clouds, fog, falling snow, sun rays, glow, bloom, particles, aircraft, shadows of aircraft, bullets, enemies, game UI, labels, text, logos, or watermarks. Clouds and weather are separate runtime layers. Final output must be one finished original portrait terrain painting with an opaque background.

Use case: stylized-concept.
Asset type: one original opaque 1024x1536 portrait terrain tile for a high-altitude top-down airplane scrolling shooter. One complete finished painting, no contact sheet or UI.

Image 1 is the accepted icefield-and-igloo tile. Image 2 is the approved first-stage painted island style. Use both as STYLE AND AERIAL SCALE references. Create a NEW COMPOSITION for the next icefield segment, not an enlarged detail, duplicate scene, or recoloring of the reference. Match Image 1's slate-cyan ice, ivory snow, shallow blue ice edges, soft upper-left lighting, hand-painted planes, and modest miniature details. Keep the same near-top-down 75–80 degree aerial camera, no horizon, no large front-facing walls.

This variation is a broad fractured ice shelf. The central playable area remains largely SOLID, quiet, desaturated blue ice with a few fine irregular fractures and small soft frost patches. An irregular, branching dark-navy water fissure enters from the middle LEFT edge, bends up along that edge, and breaks into a few low, flat ice plates. It never forms a straight canyon or a full-height central river. On the right, asymmetrical low snow-covered ice terraces extend into the frame at different depths, with shallow edges and a handful of low rocks. Several flat blue ice slabs sit beside the LEFT fissure, with wide spacing and shadows that fit the same light source. Do not densely fill the center with white debris.

No buildings in this variation. No igloos, tents, trees, decorative crystal spires, large mountains, vehicles, bridges or roads. Keep scenery small relative to the broad icefield. Top and bottom edges should be simple quiet blue ice through the central 55 percent and pale snow/ice shelves towards the outer left and right 15–20 percent, similar to Image 1, allowing a scrolling transition without horizontal bars. Vary the snow outlines naturally. Avoid mirrored banks or repeated identical shapes.

Paint the ice surface with broad calm material planes and restrained scattered thin cracks. Reduce noisy white frost speckling compared with Image 1, so white aircraft and bullets remain legible. Snow is shaded ivory and silver-blue, not pure white. A few thin pale cyan rim reflections on fractures are enough; no emissive cracks, neon, lava flow, ocean waves, or caustic patterns. No pasted stickers: all shelves, rocks, snow and shadows belong to the same painted terrain.

Do not bake clouds, fog, snowfall, bloom, sun beams, aircraft, enemies, bullets, labels, text, logos, borders or watermarks into the image. Return one original opaque portrait terrain painting, edge to edge.

Use case: stylized-concept.
Asset type: one original opaque 1024x1536 portrait environment tile for a high-altitude top-down airplane scrolling shooter. One complete finished painting, no contact sheet or UI.

Image 1 is the accepted icefield-and-igloo tile. Image 2 is the approved first-stage painted island style. Use them as STYLE AND AERIAL SCALE references, keeping the same muted slate-cyan solid ice, ivory/silver-blue snow, soft upper-left daylight, clean painted brush planes and miniature environmental scale. Create a NEW composition for a different scrolling segment. Near-top-down high aerial camera, around 75–80 degrees downward, no horizon; roofs and upper surfaces dominate with only low building sides visible.

This is the polar field-station segment of the icefield. A broad, quiet old blue ice sheet occupies the central 55–65 percent, with a few thin discontinuous cracks and broad frost patches rather than a dense noisy web. Low snow platforms enter from the sides at offset positions. In the upper-right side, place a tiny grounded polar research camp on a low snow shelf: two squat gray-blue prefabricated cabins partly banked in snow, a small roof radar dish, a few short antenna masts, an orange covered supply bundle, and small warm windows. The ENTIRE station occupies around 12–16 percent of image width, and each cabin is only around 4–6 percent wide. Avoid a giant main building, large vertical facade, tall tower, or large foreground installation.

On a separate lower-left snow shelf, include a very small expedition camp of two low muted orange/gray fabric tents, a tiny sled and a few close-packed supplies. Faint short tracks link only nearby objects. All buildings, tents and supplies are anchored into the same snow painting with partly buried bases and coherent contact shadows. No people or large characters. No vehicles, roads, lane markings, helipads or oversized emblems.

Add a narrow, irregular dark-blue fracture near the right edge in the lower half, with a few flat broken ice pieces. Keep the middle primarily frozen ice, not open river water. Low rounded drift formations and sparse exposed rocks form asymmetric shore-like snow margins, not two identical straight banks. No forest, pine trees, decorative crystals, towering cliffs or mountains. Objects remain small enough to convey a high flight altitude.

For scrolling continuity, keep top and bottom edges visually simple: muted blue ice across the central 55 percent, low snow shelves towards the outer sides, similar values and scale to Image 1. No wide horizontal road, dark bar, seam, frame or border. Do not cut an important building across the image edge. Clean readable hand-painted game environment, lightly volumetric without plastic toy shading or photographic microtexture.

Do not bake in clouds, fog, snowflakes, bloom, glow, aircraft, aircraft shadows, enemies, bullets, text, labels, logos or watermarks. Return one original opaque portrait terrain painting, filling the whole image.

notes: Original generated art, no original-game media. Ice and buildings share one painted terrain plane; first-stage cloud textures are independent. No simulation or numerical gameplay change.
